To figure out the perimeter of the region bounded by the curve traced out by the incenter of triangle \( ABC \), we start by recalling a crucial geometric property: the incenter of a triangle is the intersection of the angle bisectors of the triangle. Denote the circle as centered at \( O \) with radius \( 9 \). As point \( C \) moves on this circle, the center \( O' \) of the incircle of triangle \( ABC \) moves around, tracing a circular path.

The radius of the circle traced out by \( O' \) is given by the Apollonius Circle Properties: The circle traced by the incenters of triangles sharing a common base when the vertices of the opposite angles move on a given circle has a radius that is equal to the altitude of the triangle. For the base \( AB = 18 \) and defining \( h \) as the distance from \( C \) to \( AB \), which varies between \( 0 \) and \( 18 \), the radius of the circle traced by \( O' \) monotonically decreases from the apothem to 0.

The radius of the circle traced by \( O' \) is given by \( h \), which is a function of the position of \( C \). As \( C \) moves from \( A \) to \( B \) and back (assuming tracing in a continuous manner), this radius covers a circular path of length equal to the height of \( \triangle ABC \) on the altitude from \( C \), each time \( C \) is at a point equidistant on each side of \( AB \). Thus, for each semicircle or one full circle, within the bounds defined by the centers' apex \( h \), the paths overlap, and we seek the radius containing two points (doubled).

This peculiar property results in half the previous circle traced. Since \( h \) ranges from top to bottom direction (a diameter length minimum circle per semicircle movement around \( AB \)), returning to \( O' \) again equates the doubled of \( AO' + BO' \) covering \( C \). The apex height reaches \( \frac{18 \sqrt{3}}{2} = 9 \sqrt{3} \), and starting.

Now we apply:
\[ \, 2 \times \left( 9\ \text{circle radius}\right)\,
\]

\) Our ring is thus subsumed:
\boxed{9\sqrt{3}\times 16}
